entry.title: Testing Android Backup and Restore with AndroidX
entry.content:
Getting a new phone is exciting. You take it out of the box, peel off the protective film, and sign in. Your apps begin downloading, your wallpaper shows up, and before long it looks like your phone again.

You open an app. Sign in. Open another one. Sign in again. What was the password for this one? Now you’re digging through your password manager and waiting for verification codes.

Even after you’re signed in, things aren’t quite right. Your settings are back to their defaults. The book you were reading has forgotten your page. The draft you hadn’t finished is gone. The app made it to your new phone, but it doesn’t feel like your app anymore.

Google is pushing developers to fix this. Its August app quality announcement says that starting in April 2027, apps with sign-in will need to support restoring sign-in with the Restore Credentials API to keep Play Store visibility.

Getting the user signed back in is one half of the problem. Getting their data back is the other half, and in my experience it’s the half that quietly breaks. Someone adds a new preferences file and forgets to update the backup rules. An installation ID gets copied to a new device, and now two phones look like the same install. Data encrypted with an Android Keystore key gets restored onto a device that doesn’t have that key, and the app crashes on first launch. None of these show up in a normal unit test.

Fortunately, AndroidX now has a backup testing library that lets us automate the whole round trip. Let’s take a look.

Testing it the old way

Before this library, testing backup meant running a few adb commands by hand, roughly following the backup testing guide:

adb shell bmgr enable true
adb shell bmgr backupnow com.example.backupdemo
adb uninstall com.example.backupdemo
adb install app-debug.apk

Then you’d open the app and poke around to see whether your data came back. That works, but it’s manual, it’s easy to forget, and “poke around” isn’t a great assertion. It’s the kind of check that gets done once when backup is first set up and never again.

How the library works

The library splits the test into two halves:

  • backup-host runs on your development machine (or CI) and drives the whole process over ADB: run some code in the app, trigger a backup, wipe the app’s data, restore it, run more code.
  • backup runs inside the app on the device. This is where you write data before the backup and check it afterwards.

Why split things up? Clearing app data kills the process that would normally be running your instrumentation test. Keeping the orchestration on your computer lets the test keep going across that wipe and pick back up inside the restored app.

Android decides what gets backed up, based on your app’s backup rules. The library doesn’t fake any of that; it just gives you a way to test the rules you’ve written.

Version note: This post uses 1.0.0-alpha01, released September 23, 2026. It’s an early alpha, so expect some of this to change. Check the release notes if you’re on a newer version.

Decide what should come back

Before writing any test code, it’s worth writing down what should survive a restore. It’s tempting to check that everything comes back and call it a day, but restoring the wrong thing is a bug too.

For this post, let’s use a reading app that lets you take notes:

  • Should come back: the current book and page, plus the user’s notes.
  • Should stay behind: an installation ID that’s generated fresh on each install.

When you do this for your own app, a few things almost always belong in the “stay behind” list:

  • Installation IDs, push tokens, and other per-device identifiers
  • Anything encrypted with a Keystore key, since Keystore keys don’t move to the new device
  • Auth tokens, which should go through Restore Credentials instead of a file backup
  • Caches that can just be rebuilt

For an app targeting API 31 or higher, point the manifest at the Android 12+ rules, and keep the legacy rules for older devices:

<application
    android:allowBackup="true"
    android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules"
    android:fullBackupContent="@xml/backup_rules" />

In res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml:

<data-extraction-rules>
    <cloud-backup>
        <include domain="sharedpref" path="." />
        <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="device_state.xml" />
        <include domain="file" path="notes/" />
    </cloud-backup>
    <device-transfer>
        <include domain="sharedpref" path="." />
        <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="device_state.xml" />
        <include domain="file" path="notes/" />
    </device-transfer>
</data-extraction-rules>

Cloud backup and device-to-device transfer have separate rule sets, so you need to configure both. One thing that trips people up: once you add an include, only the included locations are backed up for that rule set. The Auto Backup documentation covers the defaults and the available domains.

And the legacy version in res/xml/backup_rules.xml:

<full-backup-content>
    <include domain="sharedpref" path="." />
    <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="device_state.xml" />
    <include domain="file" path="notes/" />
</full-backup-content>

The test below runs on an API 31+ device, so it only exercises the modern rules. If you care about the legacy rules, you’ll want to test those on an older device separately.

Setting up the tests

You’ll need a disposable, unlocked device or emulator running API 31 or higher. And I mean disposable: the test wipes your app’s data, including once before it starts. For the cloud and device-transfer modes, use a debuggable build and an emulator image with Google Play services.

The app module

In the app module’s build.gradle.kts:

android {
    defaultConfig {
        testApplicationId = "com.example.backupdemo.test"
        testInstrumentationRunner =
            "androidx.test.backup.BackupRestoreTestRunner"
    }
}

dependencies {
    androidTestImplementation("androidx.test.backup:backup:1.0.0-alpha01")
}

Two things to watch out for here:

  1. In alpha01, the host expects the test APK’s package to be exactly <applicationId>.test. If your debug build adds an application ID suffix, account for it in both places: testApplicationId here, and @BackupRestoreConfig(applicationId) in the host test.
  2. BackupRestoreTestRunner replaces your normal instrumentation runner. If you already have Espresso or Compose UI tests in this module, you’ll probably want a dedicated build variant for backup tests.

The host module

Next, add a plain Kotlin/JVM module named backup-host-tests and include it in settings.gradle.kts. Here’s its build.gradle.kts (if your root build already declares the Kotlin JVM plugin, drop the version here):

plugins {
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.2.21"
}

kotlin { jvmToolchain(17) }

dependencies {
    testImplementation("androidx.test.backup:backup-host:1.0.0-alpha01")
    testImplementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core:1.10.2")
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.11.4"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
    testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
    outputs.upToDateWhen { false }
    outputs.cacheIf { false }
    val serial = providers.gradleProperty("backupSerial")
    doFirst {
        val value = serial.orNull
        require(!value.isNullOrBlank()) { "Pass -PbackupSerial=<serial>" }
        systemProperty("androidx.test.backup.device.serial", value)
    }
}

The host tests use JUnit 5, so this module needs the JUnit Platform setup above. I’m also doing two things that aren’t strictly required, but that I’d recommend:

  • Requiring a device serial. This test wipes app data, so I’d rather it fail loudly than wipe whatever device happens to be plugged in.
  • Turning off up-to-date checks and caching. Changing your backup rules and reinstalling doesn’t change anything in this module, so without these lines Gradle will skip the test and report it as passing.

Writing the device actions

The device side is made up of actions: small classes that the host asks the app to run. Each one needs a public no-argument constructor so the runner can create it, and the Context it gets belongs to your app.

Put these in the app’s src/androidTest/java/com/example/backupdemo/BackupActions.kt. First, an action that writes our test data:

package com.example.backupdemo

import android.content.Context
import androidx.test.backup.BackupDeviceAction
import androidx.test.backup.BackupDeviceActionArgs
import androidx.test.backup.BackupDeviceActionResult
import java.io.File

class SeedReadingState : BackupDeviceAction {
    override val phase = BackupDeviceAction.PHASE_POPULATE

    override fun execute(
        context: Context,
        args: BackupDeviceActionArgs,
    ): BackupDeviceActionResult {
        check(context.getSharedPreferences("reading_progress", 0).edit()
            .putString("book", "the-hobbit")
            .putInt("page", 137)
            .commit())
        check(context.getSharedPreferences("device_state", 0).edit()
            .putString("installation_id", "old-installation")
            .commit())
        val note = File(context.filesDir, "notes/current.txt")
        check(note.parentFile!!.isDirectory || note.parentFile!!.mkdirs())
        note.writeText("Thoughts about chapter seven")
        return BackupDeviceActionResult()
    }
}

Note that we’re using commit() instead of apply(), so the data is definitely on disk before the backup starts. In a real app you’d use whatever persistence you actually use (Room, DataStore, etc.), but the same rule applies: make sure the writes have finished.

Next, an action that checks the data. We’ll run it three times: right after seeding, after wiping, and after restoring. The host tells it which one via a stage argument:

class VerifyReadingState : BackupDeviceAction {
    override val phase = BackupDeviceAction.PHASE_VERIFY

    override fun execute(
        context: Context,
        args: BackupDeviceActionArgs,
    ): BackupDeviceActionResult {
        val stage = args.payload.getValue("stage")
        val progress = context.getSharedPreferences("reading_progress", 0)
        val device = context.getSharedPreferences("device_state", 0)
        val note = File(context.filesDir, "notes/current.txt")

        when (stage) {
            "seeded", "restored" -> {
                check(progress.getString("book", null) == "the-hobbit") {
                    "Wrong or missing book at $stage"
                }
                check(progress.getInt("page", -1) == 137) {
                    "Wrong or missing page at $stage"
                }
                check(note.exists() &&
                    note.readText() == "Thoughts about chapter seven") {
                    "Wrong or missing note at $stage"
                }
            }
            "cleared" -> {
                check(!progress.contains("book")) { "Book survived clear" }
                check(!progress.contains("page")) { "Page survived clear" }
                check(!note.exists()) { "Note survived clear" }
            }
            else -> error("Unknown stage: $stage")
        }

        if (stage == "seeded") {
            check(device.getString("installation_id", null) == "old-installation")
        } else {
            check(!device.contains("installation_id")) {
                "Installation ID should be absent at $stage"
            }
        }
        return BackupDeviceActionResult()
    }
}

Checking all three stages might look like overkill, but each one guards against a test that passes for the wrong reason:

  • Seeded proves the installation ID existed. Otherwise the “it didn’t come back” check would pass even if we never wrote it.
  • Cleared proves the wipe worked, so whatever we see afterwards really came from the restore.
  • Restored is the one we care about.

If your app generates a new installation ID on startup, change the cleared and restored checks to assert that the ID isn’t "old-installation", rather than that it’s missing.

Wiring it all together

Now for the host side. In backup-host-tests/src/test/kotlin/com/example/backupdemo/ReadingStateBackupTest.kt:

package com.example.backupdemo

import androidx.test.backup.host.BackupActionResult
import androidx.test.backup.host.BackupRestoreConfig
import androidx.test.backup.host.BackupRestoreController
import androidx.test.backup.host.BackupRestoreExtension
import androidx.test.backup.host.BackupTransportMode
import java.nio.file.Path
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith
import org.junit.jupiter.api.io.TempDir

@ExtendWith(BackupRestoreExtension::class)
@BackupRestoreConfig(applicationId = "com.example.backupdemo")
class ReadingStateBackupTest {
    @TempDir
    lateinit var outputDir: Path

    @Test
    fun readingStateSurvives(controller: BackupRestoreController) {
        runBlocking {
            suspend fun action(name: String, stage: String = "") {
                val result = controller.runOnDevice(
                    actionClassName = "com.example.backupdemo.$name",
                    args = mapOf("stage" to stage),
                )
                check(result is BackupActionResult.Success) {
                    "$name ($stage) failed: $result"
                }
            }

            action("SeedReadingState")
            action("VerifyReadingState", "seeded")
            controller.stopApp()
            val archive = controller.performBackup(
                mode = BackupTransportMode.CLOUD_ENCRYPTED,
                outputDir = outputDir,
            )
            controller.clearAppData()
            action("VerifyReadingState", "cleared")
            controller.performRestore(archive)
            action("VerifyReadingState", "restored")
        }
    }
}

I like how this reads: it’s the same sequence as the real thing. Write data, back up, wipe, restore, check. When it fails, the failure message tells you which step and which piece of data went wrong.

A few notes on the details:

  • BackupRestoreExtension injects the BackupRestoreController, and its APIs are suspending, which is why everything is wrapped in runBlocking.
  • The little action() helper checks every result. When a check() throws on the device, the host gets back a failure result, not an exception, so if you forget to check the result your test will pass no matter what happened on the device.

Running it (and breaking it)

Build and install both APKs, then run the host tests. Grab your device’s serial from adb devices. These paths assume a standard app module without product flavors:

./gradlew :app:assembleDebug :app:assembleDebugAndroidTest
adb -s emulator-5554 install -r app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
adb -s emulator-5554 install -r -t app/build/outputs/apk/androidTest/debug/app-debug-androidTest.apk
./gradlew :backup-host-tests:test -PbackupSerial=emulator-5554

Once it passes, break it on purpose. A test you’ve never seen fail hasn’t proven much yet.

  1. Add <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="reading_progress.xml" /> to the cloud-backup rules, rebuild, reinstall, and rerun. The book/page check should fail after restore.
  2. Put that back, then remove the device_state.xml exclusion. Now the installation ID check should fail.
  3. Restore the original rules.

If both of those fail the way you’d expect, you can trust the test to catch the regressions you actually care about.

Other transport modes

The test above uses CLOUD_ENCRYPTED, but you can swap in CLOUD_UNENCRYPTED or DEVICE_TO_DEVICE to test the other paths. There’s also LOCAL, which is handy as a quick smoke test, but the archive it gives you isn’t a real portable backup.

It’s worth being clear about what these modes don’t do: they simulate the backup policies, but they don’t send anything to a real Google account or a real second phone.

Running in CI

A couple of tips if you want to run this in CI:

  • Run backup tests one at a time per device. Backup configuration is shared device state, so parallel runs will trip over each other.
  • Put a timeout on the whole CI job. The library has its own timeout settings, but it’s an alpha, and I wouldn’t rely on them alone to keep a hung device from eating your build minutes.

Wrap-up

Backup is one of those features that’s easy to forget about, because nothing tells you it’s broken. You usually find out from a one-star review written by someone who just got a new phone.

I wouldn’t try to cover every file in your app on day one. I’d pick the one or two things your users would be most annoyed to lose (their place in a book, their notes, their settings) and the one or two things that should never follow them (installation IDs, anything tied to the Keystore), and write a test for those. Once that’s in place, adding a check is a few lines every time someone adds a new preferences file.

Combined with Restore Credentials for sign-in, that gets you a lot closer to an app that just picks up where the user left off. Hopefully it saves a few of your users an evening of setting things up again!

entry.title: How to Combine PagingData with Other Flows Using asItemSnapshotListFlow
entry.content:
If you’ve ever tried to combine a Flow<PagingData<T>> with another Flow, you’ve probably discovered that PagingData doesn’t behave like a regular list of items.

That’s by design. PagingData is meant to be consumed by Paging’s presenters, like PagingDataAdapter or LazyPagingItems. Those presenters know how to listen for page events, trigger more loads as the user scrolls, and update the UI as new items arrive.

But sometimes your screen needs the currently loaded items as state. Maybe you want to combine them with selected IDs, optimistic likes, or locally edited titles. This has been a common source of confusion for developers trying to combine PagingData with another Flow, expose paging from an MVI-style screen (one where the UI renders a single state object), or update loaded items without forcing a full refresh.

Paging 3.5.0 adds a new API for this: asItemSnapshotListFlow.

The new shape: loaded items as state

At its simplest, the new API looks like this:

val itemsFlow: Flow<ItemSnapshotList<Post>> =
    pager.flow.asItemSnapshotListFlow()

Each emission gives you the currently loaded items in snapshot.items, along with counts of any placeholders before and after them. You can read and transform that list anywhere you collect the flow.

One heads-up before we go further: reading from a snapshot doesn’t tell Paging to load more, and append() and prepend() are the only way to do it with this API. If you render these items yourself, you’ll need to call them. We’ll get to that in Loading more data.

Combining loaded items with other state

Suppose you have a feed of posts. The posts come from Paging, but the screen also tracks a few other things: which posts the user has liked, and which authors they’ve muted.

Here’s the obvious first attempt:

val feed: Flow<PagingData<PostUiModel>> =
    combine(pager.flow, likeOverrides) { pagingData, overrides ->
        pagingData.map { post ->
            post.toUiModel(isLiked = overrides[post.id] ?: post.isLiked)
        }
    }

It compiles, and then it crashes:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Attempt to collect twice from pageEventFlow,
which is an illegal operation. Did you forget to call
Flow<PagingData<*>>.cachedIn(coroutineScope)?

When likeOverrides changes, combine hands the same PagingData to your UI again, and Paging won’t let it be collected twice. Adding cachedIn before the combine fixes it, and for simple per-item transforms like this one, that’s a perfectly good answer.

It gets awkward when you need to treat the loaded items as data. Looking one up by ID or filtering by state that lives in another Flow both mean working inside PagingData’s transform operators. asItemSnapshotListFlow gets you out of that:

val feed: Flow<List<PostUiModel>> =
    combine(
        pager.flow.asItemSnapshotListFlow(),
        likeOverrides,
        mutedAuthorIds,
    ) { snapshot, overrides, mutedIds ->
        snapshot.items
            .filterNot { post -> post.authorId in mutedIds }
            .map { post ->
                post.toUiModel(isLiked = overrides[post.id] ?: post.isLiked)
            }
    }

That’s an ordinary Flow of lists. Paging still loads incrementally, but the code doing the combining only sees what’s loaded right now.

It’s a good fit for UI-only state: selection, muted rows, expanded or collapsed sections, local filters. None of that belongs in your database or network model. It’s just how this screen reads the loaded items.

Optimistic likes and local display edits

When a user taps a like button, you want the UI to update right away, even while the network request is still running. The same goes for editing a display title locally before saving.

Historically, Paging pushed you toward updating the backing data source and invalidating the PagingSource. That’s still the right answer for durable data. But for a temporary visual change, going through a full paging refresh is a lot of ceremony for a heart icon.

With asItemSnapshotListFlow, you can keep local overlays separate and apply them to the loaded snapshot:

private val likeOverrides = MutableStateFlow<Map<PostId, Boolean>>(emptyMap())
private val localTitles = MutableStateFlow<Map<PostId, String>>(emptyMap())

val feedUiModels: Flow<List<PostUiModel>> =
    combine(
        pager.flow.asItemSnapshotListFlow(),
        likeOverrides,
        localTitles,
    ) { snapshot, overrides, titles ->
        snapshot.items.map { post ->
            post.toUiModel(
                isLiked = overrides[post.id] ?: post.isLiked,
                title = titles[post.id] ?: post.title
            )
        }
    }

fun setLiked(id: PostId, liked: Boolean) {
    likeOverrides.update { it + (id to liked) }
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try {
            repository.setLiked(id, liked)
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            likeOverrides.update { it - id }
        }
    }
}

fun editTitleLocally(id: PostId, title: String) {
    localTitles.update { it + (id to title) }
}

These overlays don’t replace your source of truth. If the request succeeds, you still need to update your backing data source, and once the refreshed item comes back with the new value you can drop the override so it can’t mask a later change from the server. If the request fails, drop it right away, as setLiked does above.

The payoff is that your UI doesn’t wait on Paging to show a local change.

Loading more data

As mentioned up top, append() and prepend() are how you load more when you work from snapshots. Here’s the shape in a ViewModel:

class FeedViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val pager = Pager(
        config = PagingConfig(pageSize = 40),
        pagingSourceFactory = pagingSourceFactory
    )

    val posts: Flow<ItemSnapshotList<Post>> =
        pager.flow.asItemSnapshotListFlow()

    fun append() {
        pager.append()
    }

    fun prepend() {
        pager.prepend()
    }
}

Then call them from your UI when the user nears an edge of the list. The 3.5.0-alpha01 release notes show a Compose example that puts a LaunchedEffect calling append() in an item at the end of the LazyColumn.

The 3.5.0 release notes also list Pager.refresh() and Pager.retry() for recovering from load errors when you work from snapshots.

Wrap-up

For a straightforward paged list, I’d still reach for collectAsLazyPagingItems() or PagingDataAdapter, since they handle scroll-driven loading for you.

I’d use asItemSnapshotListFlow when the screen needs local edits, filters from another Flow, or lookups across the loaded items. You get a list you can work with using the Flow operators you already know.

It does come with a couple of tradeoffs. Every emission gives you the whole loaded list, so any overlay change re-maps all of it, which is worth keeping in mind for very large lists. And you’re responsible for loading more pages when you render snapshots yourself.

entry.title: Adding Scrollbars to Jetpack Compose
entry.content:
Update (February 25, 2026): The scroll indicator API described in this post was reverted in Compose Foundation 1.11.0-alpha06. According to the changelog, the revert was because of API Council feedback, so we’ll likely get a new version of the API before long. In the meantime, this article still applies to Foundation 1.11.0-alpha01 through alpha05, and the concepts might carry over when the replacement lands.

Jetpack Compose Foundation 1.11-alpha-01 introduced a long-awaited feature: the ability to add custom scroll indicators to scrollable containers. If you’ve been following Compose development, you’ve probably noticed that scrollbars were conspicuously absent — unlike Android Views, which have had them built-in for years. This has been a frequently asked question on Stack Overflow and discussed in the Android developer community, and it’s been on the Compose roadmap since at least September 2024 (though the roadmap may have changed by the time you’re reading this).

Why scroll indicators matter

Scrollbars have been around for decades and are an effective, interactive UI control. As Blake Watson points out, scrollbars provide immediate visual feedback that’s hard to replicate:

  • They indicate scrollability — Users can instantly see that content extends beyond the visible area
  • They show content length — The scrollbar’s size relative to the track gives a sense of how much content exists
  • They show current position — Users know exactly where they are in the document
  • They show visible range — The thumb size indicates how much of the total content is currently visible

Without scroll indicators, users in Compose apps have been left guessing about scrollable content, especially in long lists or documents. The new APIs finally give us the tools to address this.

Background: The missing scrollbar

Compose has always lacked built-in scroll indicators. While you could build custom solutions using drawWithContent and LazyListState.layoutInfo (as many developers have done), there was no official, supported API. This gap became more noticeable as Compose matured and developers expected feature parity with Views.

Interestingly, the foundation for scroll indicators was laid quietly in version 1.10.0-alpha04, when ScrollIndicatorState was added to both LazyListState (Android review) and ScrollState (Android review). This state object provides the necessary information — scroll offset, content size, viewport size — to render a scroll indicator, but the actual rendering API didn’t arrive until 1.11-alpha-01.

The new APIs: An overview

Foundation 1.11-alpha-01 introduces the rendering APIs for scroll indicators:

  1. Modifier.scrollIndicator — A modifier you apply to scrollable containers to add a scroll indicator
  2. ScrollIndicatorFactory — An interface that defines how the indicator looks and behaves

These work together with ScrollIndicatorState to provide the necessary information — scroll offset, content size, viewport size — needed to render a scroll indicator.

The design is clean and follows Compose patterns: you provide a factory that creates the indicator composable, and the modifier handles the rest. The factory receives the ScrollIndicatorState, which contains all the information needed to render the indicator at the correct position and size.

Basic setup: Getting started

Adding a scroll indicator is surprisingly straightforward. Here’s a minimal example:

@Composable
fun ScrollableList(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()

    val scrollbarModifier = listState.scrollIndicatorState?.let {
        Modifier.scrollIndicator(
            state = it,
            orientation = Orientation.Vertical
        )
    } ?: Modifier

    LazyColumn(
        state = listState,
        modifier = modifier
            .fillMaxSize()
            .then(scrollbarModifier)
    ) {
        items(100) { index ->
            Text(
                text = "Item $index",
                modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)
            )
        }
    }
}

That’s it! Since scrollIndicatorState is nullable, we use ?.let to conditionally create the scroll indicator modifier, then apply it with .then(). The default factory (when no factory is specified) provides a simple, functional scrollbar. The same pattern works for regular scrollable containers like Column or Row — just use rememberScrollState() instead of rememberLazyListState().

Customizing for Material 3 look

The default scroll indicator is functional but basic. If you want something that matches Material 3’s scrollbar design (like what you’d see in Views), you’ll need to create a custom ScrollIndicatorFactory. Here’s an implementation that approximates the Material 3 scrollbar, matching the constants from Android’s ViewConfiguration:

data class MaterialScrollIndicatorFactory(
    val thumbThickness: Dp = 4.dp,
    val padding: Dp = 2.dp,
    val thumbColor: Color = Color.Black,
    val thumbAlpha: Float = 0.5f,
    val fadeDelay: Int = 300, // milliseconds, matches SCROLL_BAR_DEFAULT_DELAY
    val fadeDuration: Int = 250, // milliseconds, matches SCROLL_BAR_FADE_DURATION
) : ScrollIndicatorFactory {
    override fun createNode(
        state: ScrollIndicatorState,
        orientation: Orientation
    ): DelegatableNode {
        return object : Modifier.Node(), DrawModifierNode {
            private val alpha = Animatable(0f)
            private var fadeOutJob: Job? = null

            override fun onAttach() {
                super.onAttach()

                // Monitor scroll offset changes to trigger fade animations
                coroutineScope.launch {
                    snapshotFlow { state.scrollOffset }
                        .collect { _ ->
                            // Cancel any pending fade-out
                            fadeOutJob?.cancel()

                            // Fade in immediately when scrolling
                            launch {
                                alpha.animateTo(
                                    targetValue = thumbAlpha,
                                    animationSpec = tween(
                                        durationMillis = 150,
                                        easing = FastOutSlowInEasing
                                    )
                                )
                            }

                            // Schedule fade-out with delay
                            fadeOutJob = launch {
                                delay(fadeDelay.toLong())
                                alpha.animateTo(
                                    targetValue = 0f,
                                    animationSpec = tween(
                                        durationMillis = fadeDuration,
                                        easing = FastOutSlowInEasing
                                    )
                                )
                            }
                        }
                }
            }

            override fun ContentDrawScope.draw() {
                // Draw the original content.
                drawContent()

                // Don't draw the scrollbar if the content fits within the viewport.
                if (state.contentSize <= state.viewportSize) return

                // Don't draw if fully transparent
                if (alpha.value <= 0f) return

                val visibleContentRatio = state.viewportSize.toFloat() / state.contentSize

                // Calculate the thumb's size and position along the scrolling axis.
                val thumbLength = state.viewportSize * visibleContentRatio
                val thumbPosition = state.scrollOffset * visibleContentRatio

                val thumbThicknessPx = thumbThickness.toPx()
                val paddingPx = padding.toPx()

                // Determine the scrollbar size and thumb position based on the orientation.
                val (topLeft, size) =
                    when (orientation) {
                        Orientation.Vertical -> {
                            val x = size.width - thumbThicknessPx - paddingPx
                            Offset(x, thumbPosition) to Size(thumbThicknessPx, thumbLength)
                        }
                        Orientation.Horizontal -> {
                            val y = size.height - thumbThicknessPx - paddingPx
                            Offset(thumbPosition, y) to Size(thumbLength, thumbThicknessPx)
                        }
                    }

                // Draw the scrollbar thumb with rounded corners using animated alpha.
                val cornerRadius = thumbThickness.toPx() / 2f
                drawRoundRect(
                    color = thumbColor,
                    topLeft = topLeft,
                    size = size,
                    alpha = alpha.value,
                    cornerRadius = CornerRadius(cornerRadius, cornerRadius)
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

Then use it like this:

@Composable
fun ScrollableList(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val scrollbarFactory = remember { 
        MaterialScrollIndicatorFactory(
            thumbColor = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.onSurfaceVariant
        )
    }

    val scrollbarModifier = listState.scrollIndicatorState?.let {
        Modifier.scrollIndicator(
            factory = scrollbarFactory,
            state = it,
            orientation = Orientation.Vertical
        )
    } ?: Modifier

    LazyColumn(
        state = listState,
        modifier = modifier
            .fillMaxSize()
            .then(scrollbarModifier)
    ) {
        items(100) { index ->
            Text(
                text = "Item $index",
                modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp)
            )
        }
    }
}

This implementation includes several Material 3 design characteristics:

  • Fade in/out animation — The scrollbar fades in immediately when scrolling starts (150ms) and fades out 300ms after scrolling stops, with a 250ms fade duration (matching SCROLL_BAR_FADE_DURATION and SCROLL_BAR_DEFAULT_DELAY from ViewConfiguration)
  • Thin thumb — 4dp thickness by default, matching ViewConfiguration.SCROLL_BAR_SIZE
  • Rounded corners — Half the thumb thickness for a pill-shaped appearance
  • Proper positioning — Calculates thumb position and size based on scroll offset and content/viewport ratios using snapshotFlow to reactively respond to scroll changes
  • Customizable — Configurable thickness, padding, color, and alpha values via the data class parameters

The key insight is that ScrollIndicatorState provides scrollOffset, contentSize, and viewportSize, which are all you need to calculate where the thumb should be and how big it should be.

Future speculation

Right now, this is a foundation-level API. You get the building blocks, but if you want a Material-styled scrollbar, you need to build it yourself (or use a library). Given Google’s pattern of providing Material components in the Material library, I’d be surprised if we don’t see a MaterialScrollIndicatorFactory or similar in a future Material Compose release. This would make it a one-liner to add a Material-styled scrollbar, similar to how MaterialTheme provides default styling for other components.

Until then, the foundation API gives us the flexibility to create exactly what we need, whether that’s a Material 3 look, a custom design, or something completely custom.

Conclusion

If you’re working with long lists or scrollable content where users might benefit from visual scroll feedback, give these APIs a try. Even if you stick with the default factory, you’re providing valuable UX improvements with minimal code. And if you need something more customized, the factory pattern gives you all the control you need.

Happy scrolling!

entry.title: Smooth Theme Transitions in Compose with Animated ColorSchemes
entry.content:
If your Jetpack Compose app supports light and dark themes, you’ve probably noticed the default behavior: a sudden cut between color schemes when the system UI mode changes.

I think we’ve all seen theme changes that look like this:

We can do better.

By wrapping your theme setup with some animation, we can achieve smooth transitions between light and dark themes that feel much more polished — without rebuilding your entire app structure.

The Idea: Animate the ColorScheme

Jetpack Compose’s MaterialTheme accepts a ColorScheme. If we gradually animate the colors inside that scheme when the system toggles between dark and light, we can fade the colors smoothly across the entire app.

Here’s a simplified example:

@Composable
fun AnimatedTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val targetScheme = if (darkTheme) DarkColorScheme else LightColorScheme

    val animatedScheme = targetScheme.copy(
        primary = animateColorAsState(targetScheme.primary).value,
        background = animateColorAsState(targetScheme.background).value,
        surface = animateColorAsState(targetScheme.surface).value,
        onPrimary = animateColorAsState(targetScheme.onPrimary).value,
        // Add more swatches as needed...
    )

    MaterialTheme(
        colorScheme = animatedScheme,
        typography = Typography,
        shapes = Shapes,
        content = content
    )
}

You can expand this to include all 20+ color swatches if you want — but we’ll show a better way shortly.

The Problem: Too Many Animations

Manually animating every color swatch with animateColorAsState works, but:

  • It’s verbose
  • It runs a lot of recompositions (even for unused swatches)
  • It can be hard to keep up if ColorScheme changes

A Better Approach: Animating with updateTransition

A cleaner solution is to animate all properties as part of a single Transition. That way, Compose shares the animation clock and easing, and you’re not scattering a dozen independent animation calls.

private fun defaultColorTransitionSpec(): FiniteAnimationSpec<Color> =
    tween(durationMillis = 500, easing = LinearOutSlowInEasing)

@Composable
fun AnimatedTheme(
    darkTheme: Boolean = isSystemInDarkTheme(),
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    val targetScheme = if (darkTheme) DarkColorScheme else LightColorScheme
    val transition = updateTransition(targetScheme, label = "themeTransition")

    val primary by transition.animateColor(
        label = "primary",
        transitionSpec = { defaultColorTransitionSpec() }) { it.primary }
    val background by transition.animateColor(
        label = "background",
        transitionSpec = { defaultColorTransitionSpec() }) { it.background }
    val surface by transition.animateColor(
        label = "surface",
        transitionSpec = { defaultColorTransitionSpec() }) { it.surface }
    val onPrimary by transition.animateColor(
        label = "onPrimary",
        transitionSpec = { defaultColorTransitionSpec() }) { it.onPrimary }

    val animatedScheme = targetScheme.copy(
        primary = primary,
        background = background,
        surface = surface,
        onPrimary = onPrimary
    )
    MaterialTheme(colorScheme = animatedScheme, content = content)
}

This version:

  • Uses a single Transition to group related animations
  • Shares the same easing/duration across all swatches
  • Is easier to extend or modify incrementally

After we add our animations, it will look more like this:

Final Notes

  • If you want to animate all color properties, you’ll still need to call animateColor for each one — but this pattern scales better than copy-pasting 25 animateColorAsState calls.
  • For most apps, animating just a handful of swatches (primary, background, surface, onPrimary, error) gives most of the perceived polish.
  • Avoid using reflection or deep copying here — it’s better to be explicit and in control of what’s animated.

Wrap-Up

This technique brings a much smoother feel to your app, especially if your users frequently switch between light and dark mode (or you support a manual toggle).

(Hopefully the Compose team eventually provides a helper for this boilerplate.)

Happy theming!

Sample Code

Want to try it out yourself? I’ve published a small sample project on GitHub that demonstrates both animated and non-animated theme switching:

View the sample project on GitHub

It includes the exact code from this post and the toggle UI shown in the GIFs.

entry.title: Turning Any Android Callback into a Flow with callbackFlow
entry.content:
If you’ve been working with Android for any amount of time, you’ve probably run into APIs that expose their results using callbacks or listeners. Whether it’s something like LocationManager, a custom SDK, or a third-party service like Firebase, you’re often stuck adapting old-school async patterns into your modern reactive code.

This approach is especially helpful in apps using Jetpack Compose, coroutines, or unidirectional data flow.

Fortunately, Kotlin’s callbackFlow makes this much easier. In this post, we’ll show how to wrap a listener-based API using callbackFlow, so you can collect updates as a Flow. We’ll use the Firebase Realtime Database as an example, but this pattern works for nearly anything.

The Problem: Listeners Aren’t Reactive

Here’s the classic way of listening to changes in the Firebase Realtime Database:

val postListener = object : ValueEventListener {
    override fun onDataChange(dataSnapshot: DataSnapshot) {
        val post = dataSnapshot.getValue<Post>()
        // update UI
    }

    override fun onCancelled(error: DatabaseError) {
        Log.w(TAG, "loadPost:onCancelled", error.toException())
    }
}
postReference.addValueEventListener(postListener)

This works fine — but it’s imperative and not easily composable with things like StateFlow, LiveData, or Jetpack Compose. Let’s fix that.

The Fix: Wrap It with callbackFlow

Kotlin’s callbackFlow is designed for exactly this kind of situation — where you need to bridge a listener-based API into a reactive stream.

Here’s what it looks like for Firebase:

fun Query.asFlow(): Flow<DataSnapshot> = callbackFlow {
    val listener = object : ValueEventListener {
        override fun onDataChange(snapshot: DataSnapshot) {
            trySend(snapshot).isSuccess // emit each snapshot into the Flow
        }

        override fun onCancelled(error: DatabaseError) {
            close(error.toException()) // cancel the flow on error
        }
    }

    // Start listening for updates
    addValueEventListener(listener)

    // Suspend until the flow is closed or cancelled, then clean up
    awaitClose { removeEventListener(listener) }
}

Let’s break that down:

  • callbackFlow { ... }: Gives you a coroutine-safe way to emit values (send / trySend) from a callback-based API.
  • trySend(snapshot): Emits a value into the flow. This is non-blocking and returns a ChannelResult, which we’re ignoring here.
  • close(error.toException()): If the Firebase listener is cancelled, we close the flow with the exception. This cancels any active collectors.
  • awaitClose { ... }: Suspends the coroutine until the collector stops collecting (i.e., it’s cancelled or the flow completes), and is the right place to clean up listeners or resources.

The result is a clean Flow<DataSnapshot> that behaves just like you’d want: it emits every time Firebase sends an update and automatically stops listening when the consumer stops collecting.

Consuming the Flow

You can now collect this from anywhere in your app. Here’s a quick example:

lifecycleScope.launch {
    postReference.asFlow().collect { snapshot ->
        val post = snapshot.getValue<Post>()
        // Update UI or state
    }
}

This could also be collected in a ViewModel, transformed with map, or turned into Compose State. But that’s outside the scope of this post — we just wanted to show the full round trip here.

A Note on .snapshots

If you’re using the Firebase Realtime Database, you might have seen the (relatively new) snapshots extension, which does exactly this out of the box:

postReference.snapshots.collect { snapshot -> /* ... */ }

So if you’re only dealing with Firebase, you might not need your own wrapper. But the callbackFlow approach is still incredibly useful for any API that doesn’t have a ready-made Flow extension.

Wrap-Up

callbackFlow is a powerful tool for adapting listener-based or callback-heavy APIs into clean, composable Kotlin Flows. Once you wrap something like this, you can:

  • Collect updates in your ViewModel or UI layer
  • Combine it with other Flows
  • Debounce, map, retry, or buffer updates

Firebase was just the example here — but this trick works great for things like:

  • SensorManager
  • TextWatcher
  • LocationManager
  • WebSocket libraries
  • Custom event systems

Once you get used to wrapping listeners this way, it’s hard to go back.
